blogs.title: Stop underdosing anaphylaxis: make 0.5 mg IM epinephrine the adult default
blogs.description: This post uses the case to examine the gap between guideline-recommended adult dosing (0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg IM) and real-world use of 0.3 mg auto-injectors. We’ll discuss how underdosing—especially in heavier adults and with shorter auto-injector needles—may drive repeated dosing, care escalation, and possibly multiphasic courses. Practical fixes: stocking 0.5 mg devices or prefilled syringes, weight-based order sets, training to reduce hesitancy with drawn-up epinephrine, and explicit discharge plans when only 0.3 mg auto-injectors are available (carry two, dose early, repeat promptly).

blogs.title: The second wave problem: observation windows and ICU triggers in biphasic/multiphasic anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Biphasic and multiphasic courses strain ED and ICU resources and challenge risk stratification. We’ll clarify definitions (biphasic vs refractory vs sustained), summarize timing (most recurrences within 6–12 hours but can be later), and compare guideline approaches, highlighting the UK risk-tiered model. Building from this case, we propose pragmatic criteria for extended observation or ICU admission: severe initial shock/hypoxemia, multiple epinephrine doses, comorbid mast cell disease/elevated baseline tryptase, unknown/long-acting allergen, and unreliable follow-up. We’ll end with a practical observation algorithm clinicians can adapt locally.

blogs.title: Steroids in anaphylaxis: time to break the habit
blogs.description: Despite persistent bedside use, contemporary evidence shows corticosteroids do not prevent biphasic reactions and may be associated with harm (e.g., higher admission rates). In this case, recurrences continued despite steroids. We’ll review the data, examine why steroids remain entrenched, and outline when they still may have a role (concomitant asthma exacerbation, refractory shock after adequate epinephrine and fluids, steroid-dependent conditions). Key takeaways prioritize early, adequate epinephrine, supportive care, and appropriate observation over routine steroid administration.

blogs.title: Tryptase matters: getting the right samples and spotting mast cell disease after anaphylaxis
blogs.description: This post turns a common pitfall—missed or mistimed tryptase—into a practical checklist. We’ll cover when and how to sample (early sample as soon as feasible, a 1–2 hour peak sample within 4 hours, and a baseline at least 24 hours after recovery), how to interpret using change from baseline, and when to refer for mast cell workup. Leveraging this case’s elevated baseline tryptase and features suggestive of systemic mastocytosis, we’ll discuss how underlying mast cell disorders may predispose to severe or multiphasic reactions and why getting the labs right changes long-term management.

blogs.title: When anaphylaxis won’t quit: IM repeat vs IV epinephrine infusion
blogs.description: What do you do after the second or third relapse? We’ll outline indications to transition from repeated IM epinephrine to a carefully titrated IV epinephrine infusion in a monitored setting, along with practical considerations: resuscitation readiness, infusion preparation per local protocol, continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring, and integration with fluids, oxygen, and adjuncts (e.g., glucagon if beta-blocked). We’ll contrast a pre-emptive infusion strategy with an expectant approach, using this case to map the risks, benefits, and shared decision-making with allergy/critical care teams.

blogs.title: Clarithromycin anaphylaxis in a beta-lactam–allergic patient: navigating the antibiotic allergy maze
blogs.description: Macrolide anaphylaxis is uncommon but real. This post uses the case to review antibiotic selection in skin/soft tissue infections when a penicillin allergy label exists, highlighting pitfalls of misattributed rashes, cross-reactivity myths, and the need for de-labeling pathways when safe. We’ll discuss counseling after a severe macrolide reaction (strict avoidance, documentation, medical alerting, and epinephrine auto-injector education) and practical alternatives for future infections. The goal: safer prescribing, fewer unnecessary restrictions, and better patient outcomes.
